question: Does a country's population pyramid say anything about its later economic growth, and did that growth reach an index investor? This page lists what the published literature found, what happened after a well-known case (China 1990), and what this site's own pre-registered backtest found on its own data. Nothing here is a forecast.

links.title: Age structure → GDP growth
links.summary: Across studies, a rising working-age share went with faster GDP-per-capita growth, but only where policy let it — the authors call the dividend "not inevitable", something that "has to be earned".

findings.claim: The demographic dividend accounted for as much as one-third of East Asia's economic miracle (1965–90).
findings.effect: ≈ 1/3 of East Asia's per-capita growth (Bloom, Canning & Sevilla); Bloom, Canning & Malaney (1999) give a third to a half
findings.citation: Bloom, Canning & Sevilla (2001/2003), NBER WP 8685; RAND MR-1274

findings.claim: The original one-third attribution.
findings.citation: Bloom & Williamson (1998), World Bank Economic Review 12(3):419–455

findings.claim: East Asia's working-age population grew about 2.4 %/yr, nearly four times the dependent population; the working-age share rose from about 57 % (1965) to about 68 % (2000); per-capita income grew more than 6 %/yr.
findings.effect: working-age share +11 pp over 35 years alongside > 6 %/yr per-capita income growth

findings.claim: A one-percentage-point rise in the working-age share went with about 1.5 pp faster GDP-per-capita growth.
findings.effect: +1 pp working-age share ≈ +1.5 pp GDP-per-capita growth
findings.citation: Cruz & Ahmed (2018), World Development 105:95–106; companion typology paper World Bank WPS7893

findings.claim: Openness tripled the effect: a working-age population growing 1.5 % faster than the total added about 0.5 %/yr of growth in a closed economy but about 1.5 %/yr in an open one.

Latin America grew 0.7 %/yr per capita over 1975–95 against East Asia's 6.8 % with favourable demographics from 1970; direct age-structure effects explained about 11 % of the gap, about 50 % once the policy interaction is included; only 12 % of the region counted as open by 1980.
findings.effect: 0.7 %/yr vs 6.8 %/yr; age structure alone ≈ 11 % of the gap

findings.claim: Sub-Saharan fertility fell slowly: DRC 6.1 (1960) → 6.0 (2024); Nigeria 6.4 → 4.4; Uganda 6.9 → 4.2; DRC's dependency ratio rose from 84.8 to 96.5.

This project's earlier backcast: effective-labour growth against realised 2000–2020 GDP growth over 69 countries — correlation 0.47, slope 0.76, MAE 1.5 pp; worst misses China, Vietnam, Ethiopia (catch-up growth dominated).

links.title: GDP growth → equity returns
links.strength: negative across countries over a century
links.summary: Across countries, faster real GDP-per-capita growth went with LOWER real equity returns; growth financed by new capital accrued to new shareholders and expected growth was already in prices.

findings.claim: Cross-country correlation of real GDP-per-capita growth with real equity returns was negative.
findings.citation: Dimson, Marsh & Staunton (2002), Triumph of the Optimists

findings.claim: Cross-country correlation of real GDP-per-capita growth with real equity returns: −0.37.
Correlation −0.39 (p ≈ .10); −0.32 in USD terms.
findings.citation: Ritter (2012), Journal of Applied Corporate Finance

findings.claim: Correlation −0.41 in emerging markets.
findings.citation: Ritter (2012), Journal of Applied Corporate Finance

findings.claim: No significant relationship in a wider sample.
findings.citation: Dimson, Marsh & Staunton, Credit Suisse Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2010

findings.claim: Mechanism: growth from added capital and labour accrued to new shareholders (dilution); investors overpaid for expected growth, and that overpayment more than offset the benefit of unexpected growth.

MSCI Barra confirmed the negative cross-country correlation; over 1969–2009 the mean slippage from GDP growth to EPS growth was 2.3 pp, offset by 2.0 pp of P/E expansion; Sweden's index beat its GDP growth by 3.5 pp/yr while Spain's trailed by 4.5 pp/yr; results flipped with a one-year endpoint shift.
findings.effect: slippage 2.3 pp; P/E offset 2.0 pp; Sweden +3.5, Spain −4.5 pp/yr
findings.citation: MSCI Barra (May 2010), 'Is There a Link Between GDP Growth and Equity Returns?'

findings.claim: China GDP per capita (PPP, constant 2021 $, WDI) went from $1,667 (1990) to $23,841 (2024), 14.3×, while the MSCI China index returned +1.55 %/yr (USD, gross) since 1992-12-31 with a maximum drawdown of 88.63 % (1993-12-31 → 2001-09-12); MSCI EM +7.89 %/yr and MSCI ACWI +9.24 %/yr over their factsheet windows.
findings.sample: China 1990–2024; MSCI China since 1992-12-31 (factsheet as of 2026-08-31)
findings.citation: WDI; MSCI China Index factsheet (accessed 2026-09-04) — the transcribed values are in evals/econ/msci_citations.yaml

links.title: Demographics → equity returns directly
links.summary: Direct age-structure models of equity returns existed and mostly failed out of sample; the historical record has too few effective degrees of freedom for sharp tests.

findings.claim: Polynomial cohort-share model: +1 % in the 50–54 cohort went with about +1 pp of annual equity return, +1 % in the 70+ cohort with about −1.5 pp.
'Statistical tests have limited power based on the few effective degrees of freedom in the historical record'; no sharp prospective decline implied.
findings.citation: Poterba (2001), Review of Economics and Statistics 83(4):565–584

findings.claim: The MY ratio (ages 40–49 / 20–29) moved with stock prices in an overlapping-generations model.
findings.citation: Geanakoplos, Magill & Quinzii (2004), Brookings Papers on Economic Activity

findings.claim: An M/O-ratio model forecast the US P/E falling to about 8.4 by 2025; it failed out of sample.
findings.effect: forecast P/E ≈ 8.4 by 2025 — did not happen
findings.citation: Liu & Spiegel (2011), FRBSF Economic Letter (follow-ups 2014 and later)

links.title: Investability
links.summary: The countries whose 2024 age structure is closest to China 1990 mostly had no US-listed single-country fund; several funds that existed were liquidated, and one index deleted a whole market at an effectively zero price.

findings.claim: The 2024 age split closest to China 1990 (0–14 28.8 % / 15–64 65.9 % / 65+ 5.3 %): Philippines, Bangladesh, Nepal, Laos, Cambodia, Jordan — not Nigeria, Ethiopia or DRC, which are younger than China ever was (DRC median age 15.9, Uganda 17.1 vs China's 1975 trough of 19.1).
findings.effect: structural matches are 5–6× richer; income matches carry dependency ratios 73–97

findings.claim: No US-listed single-country ETF existed (as of 2026-09-04) for Bangladesh, Pakistan (since 2024), Nigeria (since 2024), Ethiopia, Kenya, Egypt (since 2024), Tanzania, Uganda, DR Congo, Nepal, Laos or Cambodia; live examples: INDA, EPHE, EIDO, VNM, THD, EWY, MCHI, KSA, EPOL, AFK.
findings.effect: 12 of the young lookalikes without a fund

findings.claim: MSCI deleted every Nigerian security from the MSCI Frontier Markets Indexes at a price that is effectively zero as of the close of 29 February 2024 (foreign-exchange repatriation failures since 2020); Nigeria was reclassified Frontier → Standalone.

MSCI classification snapshot (Aug 2023): EM = India, Indonesia, Philippines, Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Korea, China, Thailand, Brazil, Mexico; Frontier/Standalone = Vietnam, Bangladesh, Kenya, Pakistan, Nigeria, Sri Lanka, Morocco, Jordan, Kazakhstan; not in the MSCI universe: Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania, DR Congo, Nepal, Laos, Cambodia.
Yahoo Finance served stale metadata — and, for some funds, full dead histories — for delisted tickers; liveness is therefore taken only from the issuer's own status and a fresh bar (PREREG §6).
findings.sample: EGPT, NGE, PAK, FM, ERUS, RSX on 2026-09-04

china.reading: Nobody today matched China 1990 on both age structure and income; today's structural matches were 5–6× richer, today's income matches carried dependency ratios of 73–97. Egypt 1990 ($8,007) and Nigeria 1990 ($5,424) were 4.8× and 3.3× China's GDP per capita and were barely richer in 2024.

L0.what_happened: Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 1990 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew -0.5 %/yr over the following 10 years, against +1.6 %/yr for the median of all 148 candidates (N_eff = 10; 40% of them beat the median).

Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 1995 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew +2.1 %/yr over the following 10 years, against +2.6 %/yr for the median of all 150 candidates (N_eff = 10; 40% of them beat the median).

Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 2000 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew +3.6 %/yr over the following 10 years, against +2.8 %/yr for the median of all 151 candidates (N_eff = 10; 40% of them beat the median).

Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 2005 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew +4.4 %/yr over the following 10 years, against +2.5 %/yr for the median of all 152 candidates (N_eff = 10; 90% of them beat the median).

Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 2010 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew +1.6 %/yr over the following 10 years, against +1.2 %/yr for the median of all 156 candidates (N_eff = 10; 50% of them beat the median).

Among the 10 countries whose pyramid in 2015 most resembled the pre-boom prototypes, GDP per capita grew -0.3 %/yr over the following 7–8 years, against +1.4 %/yr for the median of all 157 candidates (N_eff = 10; 30% of them beat the median).
L0.null: Random sets of 10 countries did at least as well in 65% of 5000 draws (p = 0.65); sets of equally poor countries did at least as well in 98% of draws (p = 0.98).

units_note: Every %/yr market figure on this page is a compound annual growth rate, 100·(e^r − 1), the unit of the L0.vs_vt sentence; the pp/yr figures (mean excess, CIs, EW minus VT) are differences of annualised log returns, the unit of the RESULTS.md §4 and §6 tables (r = ln(exit/entry)/years).

vintage.expectation: k = 10 Jaccard(WPP 2024 set, archive set) ≥ 0.6 at every T where an archive exists (PREREG §8); Query B is the primary rule
caveats: The archive CSVs are the UN's 2020 re-export of each revision's database (member dates 2020-01-24 inside the zips), not the files distributed at the time; they already carry the 21-bin (100+) layout with populated 85–99 and 100+ cells, whereas the printed WPP 2000/2002 tables used an 80+ open bin. The figures are the revision's, the layout is the re-export's.

Only the candidates' shape vectors are of the archive's vintage. The candidate set C(T) (WPP 2024 population ≥ 1 M at T plus a growth window) and the prototype set P(T) (top-decile GDP windows; WPP 2024 pyramids) are held at the main run's values, as pre-registered, so the check isolates the demographic-revision channel and does not re-run the full backtest.

σ (sigma.json) is the WPP 2024 corpus's; the archive vectors are measured with the main run's yardstick, which is the quantity of interest (would the same rule, applied to the numbers available at T, have chosen the same countries?).

Predecessor states (Sudan (Former) → SDN; Serbia and Montenegro → SRB) stand in for successors that have no archive row; their archive vectors describe a larger territory than the WPP 2024 back-series for the successor. Candidates without any archive row (e.g. SSD in WPP 2010; TWN in WPP 2000/2002) are dropped from the archive-side set, which can only lower the Jaccard.

WPP 2000 for T = 1990/1995 and WPP 2010 for T = 2005 are what PREREG §8 prescribes (the revision current for T ≤ 2000 / ≤ 2010), not the revision current at those T's (WPP 1990/1994/2004 exist only as Excel zips and were not used).

Jaccard is a set statistic on k ids: one swapped country changes k = 10 Jaccard from 1.00 to 0.82 and k = 5 from 1.00 to 0.67; the k = 5 rows are secondary and no threshold was pre-registered for them.

manual_deviations: NGE delisting date: etf_universe.yaml (frozen) says 2023-07-28; 497 supplements dated 2023-07-14 / 2023-08-07 / 2023-09-19 / 2024-03-01 moved the closing date to 2024-03-25 (liquidation ~2024-03-29), so NGE 2023 is a full calendar year (-27.27 %) and the window arithmetic uses 2024-03-25. Yahoo's stale bar dated 2024-03-25 was the real last trade; the PREREG §6 remark about a bar 'eight months after the real last trade' was wrong about the date, not about the routing.

ERUS / RSX liquidating distributions: the universe knows only ERUS 2022-08-17 and the three RSX 2024 dates; four more ERUS distributions (2023-12-27, 2024-06-17, 2024-11-06, 2024-12-20; $4.098728/share in total incl. 2022) and RSX $0.0119 declared 2025-12-22 (held at DTCC pending an OFAC licence) were transcribed. Issuer 'total return' figures after the trading halts assume reinvestment at a residual NAV of cents (RSX 2023 +296.65 %, 2024 +421.94 %) and are flagged reinvestment_artifact — the window arithmetic uses the cash_ladder (NAV at the last regular year-end, then distributions as 0 % cash plus residual NAV) instead of compounding them.

Sources beyond N-CSR + liquidation notice (PREREG §6 names those two): PAK 2023 (+27.914 %) and ERUS 2022 (-99.844 %) and 2025 (+4.615 %) are twelve N-PORT Item B.5.a monthly returns compounded; NGE / PAK / FM / ERUS calendar years come from 485BPOS prospectus bar charts (iXBRL rr:AnnualReturnYYYY); EGPT and RSX from N-CSR financial highlights.

Not available from any issuer source: FM 2024 (December N-PORT never filed; 2024 null → the 2024-01-01..2025-01-09 span is a ladder gap), the NGE (2024-03-29) and PAK (2024-02-23) cash-out NAVs per share (final stubs after 2024-01-31 are ladder gaps), and an ERUS 2021-12-31 NAV (so the ERUS cash ladder cannot be expressed in return space after 2022; the 2022 -99.844 % mark is applied and the post-halt span is a ladder gap). Ladder gaps are held at 0 % and reported, never dropped.

deviations: Disconnect table (PREREG §5): the VT proxy of §3.5 is pre-registered only for the T = 2000 and T = 2005 windows; the fund windows CHN 1990 (FXI 2004-10-08→2020-12-31: 2000 rule); KOR 1975 (EWY 2000-05-12→2005-12-30: 2000 rule); KOR 1990 (EWY 2000-05-12→2020-12-31: 2000 rule); TWN 1970 (EWT 2000-06-23→2000-12-29: 2000 rule); THA 1985 (THD 2008-04-01→2015-12-31: 2005 rule); IND 2005 (EPI 2008-02-26→2025-12-31: 2005 rule) begin before VT's first bar (2008-06-26) on other dates, so vt_benchmark applied the nearest pre-registered weights (2000 rule for entries before 2005, else the 2005 rule) until VT's first bar — an extension of §3.5, flagged vt_proxy on every such number.

Survivorship guard (PREREG §6, assertion 4): Yahoo's daily range=max endpoint served a full multi-year history for 4 delisted ticker(s) (EGPT, FM, NGE, PAK) instead of refusing (the one-bar / no-data signature seen with the monthly interval during curation). PREREG says any assertion failure stops the build; the recorded run was `make backtest DEAD_SERIES=ok` (i.e. `scripts/fetch_etf.py --dead-series ok`), which records the failure per ticker below, DISCARDS every dead series and takes those funds' returns only from etf_manual.yaml — no number in this file uses a served dead series. The Makefile default is `DEAD_SERIES ?= fail`, the strict pre-registered stop (exit 1 after 4 A4 failures), so plain `make backtest` refuses and the deviation has to be chosen explicitly on every run.

Manual NAV ladder (PREREG §6): the ladder does not cover every day of some windows — ERUS T = 2015: 2022-12-31..2025-12-31 (post-halt cash distributions: reference NAV not transcribed); FM T = 2015: 2024-11-30..2024-12-31 (calendar year not transcribed); 2025-01-01..2025-01-09 (final stub not transcribed); NGE T = 2015: 2024-01-31..2024-03-29 (final stub not transcribed); PAK T = 2015: 2024-01-31..2024-02-23 (final stub not transcribed). Each uncovered span is held at 0 % nominal and the row is carried with status liquidated_in_window (Experiment 1) / manual_incomplete (etf_returns.csv) — never dropped, never silently completed.

ERUS T = 2015 ladder gap, quantified: the row carries the 2022 N-PORT mark (-99.844 %) with the post-halt span at 0 %, i.e. 0.39 % of the start value (-55.40 pp/yr log); against the transcriber's implied but UNSOURCED 2021-12-31 NAV of $46.00 the cash actually paid ($4.098728) plus the residual NAV ($0.0352) is 9.0 % of that NAV, i.e. 22.60 % of the start value (-14.87 pp/yr log) — the mark understates recovery by 22.2 pp of start value; the T = 2015 equal-weight basket (n = 48) would move from +7.300 to +7.322 pp/yr (+0.022 pp/yr, < 0.05 pp/yr). The implied NAV enters no statistic; sourcing a `nav_2021_12_31` would put ERUS on the same cash-ladder arithmetic as RSX.

never_does: Never combines shape distance with any economic number into a score.
Never sorts or ranks result lists by return or by growth; the cohort strip reports where a country's own growth fell among its lookalikes (median, IQR, rank), in shape order.
Never shows a price, a valuation forecast or a World Economic Outlook projection.
Never links to a broker; instrument links go only to the issuer's own notice, filing or factsheet.

Never states a growth or market claim outside the pre-registered templates granted by evals/econ/decision.json (levels L1 and L2 were not granted); table cells and chips print numbers with their window, VT beside them, and every string passes the deny list.
Never shows a market number without VT (Vanguard Total World Stock ETF) over the identical window, flagged VT-proxy before 2008-06-24.
Never redistributes the International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook or any MSCI series; MSCI facts are hand-transcribed and cited with the access date.
